lesson.title: Putting It Together: Derivatives Are Linear
lesson.summary: Combining the sum rule and the constant multiple rule shows that differentiation is a linear operation, meaning the derivative of any weighted sum of functions is the same weighted sum of their derivatives.
lesson.body:
Two of the rules covered so far, the sum rule and the constant multiple rule, can be fused into a single, more powerful statement. If f and g are differentiable functions and a and b are any constants, then the derivative of a times f(x) plus b times g(x) is a times f'(x) plus b times g'(x). This property, that differentiation respects both addition and constant scaling simultaneously, is called linearity, and it is one of the most important structural facts about the derivative.

The proof is simply the sum rule and the constant multiple rule applied back to back. Let p(x) = a f(x) + b g(x). Think of p as the sum of two pieces, a f(x) and b g(x). By the sum rule, the derivative of that sum is the derivative of the first piece plus the derivative of the second piece: p'(x) = [a f(x)]' + [b g(x)]'. Now apply the constant multiple rule to each piece individually: [a f(x)]' = a f'(x), and [b g(x)]' = b g'(x). Substituting these back in gives p'(x) = a f'(x) + b g'(x), exactly the claimed linearity property. Nothing new needed to be proven from the limit definition here, since both ingredient rules were already established rigorously in earlier chapters.

For a worked example, let h(x) = 4x^3 - 7x^2 + 2. Rewrite this as a linear combination: h(x) = 4 times x^3, plus (-7) times x^2, plus the constant 2. Using the power rule, the derivative of x^3 is 3x^2 and the derivative of x^2 is 2x. Applying linearity term by term: the derivative of 4x^3 is 4 times 3x^2, which is 12x^2. The derivative of -7x^2 is -7 times 2x, which is -14x. The derivative of the constant 2 is 0, by the constant rule. Adding these pieces gives h'(x) = 12x^2 - 14x. Check this at x = 1: h'(1) = 12(1)^2 - 14(1) = 12 - 14 = -2, obtained purely by combining the individual term derivatives with their original coefficients.

Linearity is why differentiation feels so mechanical once you have the basic rules in hand: you can process a long expression with many added and subtracted terms, each scaled by its own constant, by handling one term at a time and never worrying about terms interfering with each other. This is a genuinely special property. Many operations in mathematics do not behave this simply, for instance squaring a sum does not equal the sum of the squares, but differentiation of sums and constant multiples really does behave this cleanly.

This linearity property is precisely what makes the next chapter possible: differentiating an entire polynomial, with any number of terms of any degree, by applying the power rule to each power of x and then combining the results with linearity, without ever returning to the limit definition.

The word linear here is the same idea you may recognize from linear equations: an operation is linear when it respects both addition and scalar multiplication together, rather than just one or the other in isolation. The derivative satisfies both properties at once, which is a stronger and more useful statement than the sum rule or constant multiple rule alone. It is this combined property, more than either individual rule, that mathematicians usually mean when they describe differentiation as a linear operator acting on functions.
